timelines.reading: Dedicated payment systems that make very small online payments (cents to a few dollars) economic for buying individual content items or services across the web (Millicent, CyberCoin, BitPass, PayPal micropayments, Flattr, Blendle-style pay-per-article).
timelines.test: At least 20% of internet users in a major market routinely paying through such a micropayment system; 5% for year_5pct.
timelines.reason: Follows B. The dominant reading is the dedicated micropayment system. The decisive point is Gartner's own placement: in 2010 it still placed Internet Micropayment Systems 2-5 years from the plateau (on the Slope of Enlightenment), two years after the App Store and seven after the iTunes 99-cent store. So app-store and in-game purchases were not what the label referred to; counting them, as A does, makes the 2010 placement describe something already near mainstream. A says itself that under the dedicated-system reading the answer is never mainstream. No dedicated system (Millicent, IBM Micro Payments, BitPass, Flattr, Blendle, which moved to subscriptions in 2019) reached even 5% of internet users. Not marked abandoned, because new attempts keep appearing. A Gartner definition of the 2010 entry could not be retrieved, so this rests on the placement argument.
timelines.recheck: Opened Wikipedia 'Micropayment': it lists the dedicated systems (IBM Micro Payments, iPIN 'never widely adopted', Millicent, NetBill, Flattr, Blendle pivoting from micropayments in 2019) and attributes the term mainly to in-game virtual goods; supports the reading and null years. blog.hemartin.net/2010/08/... is dead (DNS does not resolve); the Wayback Machine was not reachable from this session (connection reset / fetch refused). Fact correction from the repo's own 2010 capture (2010.json x_time 62.5, 2010 phase boundaries 53.48/84.16): the 2010 entry sits on the Slope of Enlightenment with a 2-5 year band, not 'on the rise' as pass 1 wrote. The placement argument (still 2-5 years out in 2010, after the App Store) holds either way, so years unchanged.

timelines.reading: Organisation-deployed PKI as sold in 2002: certificate authorities issuing digital certificates to users, servers and devices for authentication, encryption and signing.
timelines.test: Routine production use by at least 20% of relevant organisations (medium and large enterprises and agencies); 5% for year_5pct.
timelines.reason: Follows B. A's denominator is wrong: 'websites serving HTTPS by default' measures the web-TLS end state, not organisations deploying PKI. It led A to a 5% year of 2013, although SSL server certificates for e-commerce and large government PKIs (the DoD Common Access Card from 2001) put organisational use well above 5% by 2000-2002. The mainstream year is a late bound. Enterprise PKI with user certificates was widely judged a disappointment through the 2000s, and no survey found shows 20% of organisations running it routinely by 2009 (the hit threshold for the 2002 claim placed at 2007). The 2015-2017 HTTPS shift is the first clearly evidenced mass use. Low certainty on the upper side: if an organisation holding any SSL certificate counted as 'using PKI', the crossing would be in the 2000s and the verdict a hit. Search found no 2006-2008 survey to settle it.
timelines.recheck: Opened Wikipedia 'Public key infrastructure': says PKI vendors found a market 'not quite the market envisioned in the mid-1990s', which 'has grown both more slowly and in somewhat different ways than were anticipated', and that the largest success is government (DISA PKI for the Common Access Card). Opened arXiv 2401.05239v2: a survey of PKI problems and national eID deployments with uneven adoption; it has no organisation-share figure, so it is context only. No page found that gives a share of organisations running PKI in 2006-2009; the pass-1 years are estimates that the pages do not contradict (5% by 2000 via SSL server certificates and government PKI; mainstream 2017 is a late bound). No search spent here.

timelines.reading: Model-driven development in the OMG MDA sense: software built from platform-independent models (UML or domain models) that tools transform into code, rather than hand-coded.
timelines.test: Routine production use (model-driven code generation) by at least 20% of software-developing organisations; 5% for year_5pct.
timelines.reason: Follows B. A's 'no measurable 5% share' is wrong. The Torchiano et al. 2012-13 survey of 155 Italian software professionals (online questionnaire February-April 2011) reports that of 155 respondents 105 model (13% always, 55% sometimes) and 44% of those 105 modellers use code generation, 16% model interpretation; so about 30% of all respondents (46 of 155) use code generation at least sometimes. With a self-selected sample and occasional use, that is still clearly above 5% before 2015, and model-based code generation was routine in automotive and embedded work from the mid-2000s. A judged the 5% floor from the Wikipedia statement that MDA never gained 'mainstream industry acceptance', which concerns 20%, not 5%. Mainstream stays null. The same survey finds only 13% of companies model 'always' and models used mainly for documentation, and the MDE literature reports low industrial adoption, so routine model-driven generation by 20% of software organisations is not shown by 2021 (the latest hit year for the claims). year_5pct 2006 is an estimate; it is bounded at no later than 2011 by the survey date. Risk: if the ~30% of respondents using code generation is read as routine use by organisations, the verdict would rise to hit.
timelines.recheck: ScienceDirect page returns 403 (also to WebFetch); opened the author copy (iris.polito.it, open-access PDF of Torchiano et al., JSS 86(8) 2013). Correction of the figure: 44% is the share of the 105 modellers who use code generation, not of companies; 46 of 50 MD* adopters use code generation, i.e. about 30% of all 155 respondents, survey run Feb-Apr 2011, self-selected Italian professionals, with use 'sometimes' counted. This still bounds year_5pct at no later than 2011 (pass-1 2006 inside the bound) and does not show routine use by 20% of organisations, so mainstream stays null. Opened arXiv 2511.06103: confirms 'relatively low level of adoption of MDE in industry', models mostly for documentation, and cites Torchiano 2013 (13% always, 53% sometimes). Years unchanged.

timelines.reading: Low-power self-organising wireless mesh networks of sensors and meters (ZigBee, WirelessHART, ISA100, RF-mesh metering) for industrial, building and utility monitoring.

Under it, consumer use was mainstream by 2007: Pew found 25% of US adults using Wikipedia in February 2007. Business use of wikis and of open-source collaborative production was routine in more than 20% of large organisations well before 2016. timelines.reading: A user's identity, profile, preferences and settings that travel with them across websites, services and devices (federated or social login, portable profiles, account-based sync of settings), the sense Gartner also used on its 2007 Consumer and 2008 PC Technologies Hype Cycles.
timelines.test: At least 20% of internet users in major markets using a portable identity or profile across sites or devices (social or federated login, account-synced settings); 5% for year_5pct.
timelines.reason: Follows B. A treats three readings as equal, but the cross-world-avatar reading is a minority one. Gartner carried 'portable personality' on its Consumer Technologies (2007) and PC Technologies (2008) Hype Cycles, which places the label with a user's identity, profile and settings moving across services and devices, not with virtual-world avatars. Under that reading, federated or social login and account-based sync were mainstream by 2012-2014: Gigya surveys of US adults aged 18-55 found 77% had used social logins in 2014, 'a 45% increase over a 2012 survey' (so about 53% in 2012), and 65.5% used them often or whenever offered in 2014 against 35% in 2012. These are vendor surveys and likely overstate use, but the margin over 20% is large. Settings sync via Google, Apple and Microsoft accounts was in mass use by 2012-2014. The 2007 claim (placed 2012) is a hit if mainstream came by 2014, which holds even if 2012 is a year early. The avatar reading would give a miss, but it did not dominate.
